To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have designed and implemented a self-stabilizing distributed algorithm for computing maximum flows in networks and that our experiments with the algorithm show that it performs as well as a nonself-stabilizing distributed implementation of a well-known centralized algorithm.
we have developed the first self-stabilizing distributed maximum flow algorithm that is provably correct for acyclic networks and performs well in practice for both acyclic and cyclic networks.

we have developed and implemented a distributed self-stabling algorithm for the maximum-flow problem that (1) is guaranteed to terminate, (2) is guaranteed to produce the correct answer, (3) requires fewer than n^2 moves, (4) is faster than an implementation of the Goldberg-Tarjan maximum flow algorithm, and (5) is guaranteed to work even in networks that have cycles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing distributed algorithms for the maximum flow computation that tolerate faults, are self-stabilizing and are guaranteed to terminate in finitely steps.

the following questions: (1) What is the computational complexity of the maximum flow problem in a dynamic environment? (2) How does the computational complexity compare to the complexity of the maximum-flow algorithm in the static case?
the design and evaluation of self-stabilizing algorithms for fundamental problems in distributed computing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the algorithm computes a maximum flow in an arbitrary network in finitey many moves, where the number of moves depends on the initial state and is bounded by a polynomial in n.

the algorithm presented in this paper computes the maximum flow for any network in a finite number of moves, that it is inherently tolerant of transient faults and that it is inherently capable of adjusting automatically to dynamic changes in topology and in other parameters of interest.
this paper presents the first self-stabilizing distributed algorithm for the maximum-flow problem that is provably correct and that performs well in practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have presented an efficient self-stabilizing distributed algorithm for the maximum-flow problem.
we have designed and implemented the first distributed self-stabilising algorithm for the Maximum Flow Problem.
we have designed, implemented, and experimentally evaluated the first distributed self-stabilization algorithm for the maximum network flow problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a distributed self-stablizing algorithm can be designed to perform well in practice.
a self-stabilizing approach can be effective in solving a fundamental graph-theoretic problem.
self-stabilization can be used to design distributed algorithms for fundamental combinatorial problems that are robust to transient faults and can automatically adjust to dynamic changes.
